ALUSI-FULL:v15p236/r3.claim: Others identify the prevailing group as the Muslim king, the youths' relatives, or town leaders; Alusi finds the first identification too narrow in number and the relatives implausible without surviving kin, while many say the king and Muslims.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p236/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p236/r4.speaker: الزجاج
ALUSI-FULL:v15p236/r4.claim: Al-Zajjaj infers that believers in resurrection prevailed because mosques are established by believers.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r1.speaker: ابن حجر
ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r1.claim: Ibn Hajar lists making graves into mosques, praying toward them, touching them, and circumambulating them among major sins; Alusi explains a mosque means praying on or toward a grave, especially one revered as a prophet's or saint's.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r2.speaker: أصحابنا
ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r2.claim: Shafiʿi jurists prohibit prayer toward prophets' and saints' graves for blessing or veneration, requiring both a revered grave and intent to pray toward it; the same logic can extend to lamps and circumambulation as acts of veneration.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r3.speaker: بعض الحنابلة
ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r3.claim: Some Hanbalis call prayer at a grave for blessing defiance of God and His Messenger, an unauthorized innovation, and a major cause of shirk; they require demolishing grave structures and removing lamps.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r4.speaker: المنهاج وشرحه
ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r4.claim: The Minhaj and its commentary disfavor plastering graves and building around them outside endowed cemeteries, except where protection is needed, and prohibit construction in endowed cemeteries; grave inscriptions are also generally disfavored.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r5.speaker: الأذرعي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r5.claim: Al-Adhraʿi argues that writing Quran on graves is forbidden because it risks disrespect through trampling, impurity, and rain; writing a name merely to identify a grave is recommended by some.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p237/r6.claim: Alusi rejects an appeal to widespread grave inscriptions as consensus: visible grave construction is even more common despite known prohibition, the practice was not universal, and any practical consensus presupposes eras when moral correction can be enforced.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r1.claim: Earlier-law arguments by Muhammad, Abu Yusuf, and al-Karkhi do not establish mosque-building on graves: earlier law binds only when recounted without condemnation, whereas the Prophet cursed those who did this.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r2.claim: The argument that this verse legislates a rule inherited from earlier communities fails: unlike explicit precedents used by jurists, it merely narrates a group's statement and intention without praising or endorsing their action.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r3.claim: Because the verse neither identifies an infallible group nor praises its plan, neither their action nor intention proves that grave mosques are lawful.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r4.claim: On the account that rulers prevailed, the first group may have been believers who wanted only to build at the cave entrance and close it; they did not bury the youths because death was uncertain and awe prevented entry.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r5.claim: If the second group is viewed favorably, their mosque may have stood near the cave or over the cave on the mountain rather than over the bodies, as reports from al-Suddi, Wahb, and Mujahid indicate.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r6.claim: Using the verse to defend grave veneration, plastered structures, hanging lamps, prayer toward graves, circumambulation, touching, or scheduled gatherings opposes God and His Messenger and invents an unauthorized religion.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r7.claim: To know the right practice, examine how the Prophet's companions treated his grave, the finest grave on earth, when visiting and greeting him.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r8.speaker: ابن عطية
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r8.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya reports a cave near Loja in Granada with bodies and a dog's remains, said locally to be the cave youths; he visited it in 504 AH and saw a nearby Roman ruin called al-Raqim.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238#2/r9.claim: Alusi says Andalusi visitors claimed the occupants were hard to count and accompanied by a dog, and he personally saw large stones in the nearby ruins; he considered Andalusia likely because Christianity was dominant there and news from distant Arabia would be unlikely without revelation.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p238/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238/r1.speaker: ابن الرفعة
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238/r1.claim: The quoted legal discussion says structures over graves in public burial grounds must be demolished, including domes, unless harm is feared, in which case the matter goes to the ruler.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p238/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238/r2.speaker: علي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p238/r2.claim: In Sahih Muslim, Ali says the Prophet sent him to erase every image and level every raised grave; Ibn al-Humam limits this to high, decorated structures built over graves.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p240/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p240/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p240/r1.claim: Reports about Ibn Abbas and Muʿawiya weaken the preference for Andalusia, since Muʿawiya never entered it; Andalusi Christians being called Romans does not help, and many locate the cave at Tarsus.

ELMALILI:18:19-22/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r10.claim: A reported account says the sent companion's coin led to his discovery and thereby brought the people to learn about the sleepers.

ELMALILI:18:19-22/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r11.claim: The sleepers themselves recognized that God's promise was true and the Hour certain when they awoke as if from graves, saw their success against the persecutors, and witnessed the mercy they had hoped for.

ELMALILI:18:19-22/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r12.claim: Their story became a proof and example for themselves and others that resurrection is certain.

ELMALILI:18:19-22/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r13.claim: The people disputed what to do with the cave companions and proposed building over them so the cave could serve as their tomb.

ELMALILI:18:19-22/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r14.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:19-22/r14.claim: Those who prevailed are identified as the party that followed the companions' cause and achieved victory over their enemies; they proposed a mosque over them.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r1.claim: The discovery benefits the people of the time by making resurrection imaginable and strengthening their faith through a visible sign and the honor shown to the believers.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r2.claim: The discoverers were believers like the sleepers, so this sign confirmed and strengthened their faith; ‘likewise’ and its comparison follow the prior verse’s usage.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r3.claim: To find something is to discover or seize it after searching; God let the town’s people find the sleepers so they would know His promise was true.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r4.claim: The object of ‘We caused them to discover’ is omitted but supplied as the townspeople from the earlier warning not to let anyone know of the sleepers.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r5.claim: God’s promise means raising the dead; seeing the sleepers removes uncertainty about how revealed doctrines work, not doubt in the truth itself.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r6.claim: A saying holds that uncertainty about the manner of resurrection crosses only a sincere believer’s mind briefly and persists only in a heretic.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p287#3/r7.claim: The time clause attaches to God’s causing the discovery and portrays the townspeople’s dispute as immediately accompanying their debate over what to do with the sleepers.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r1.claim: The townspeople debated whether the sleepers were asleep or dead, would remain alive or die, would stay in the cave or return to town, and how long they had stayed.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r2.claim: The pronoun in ‘their affair’ may refer to the sleepers’ condition or to the townspeople’s decision about what to do with them.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r3.claim: The imperfect vividly brings the dispute before the reader; the account skips details of discovery and their return to the cave because they do not carry the lesson.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r4.claim: They proposed a structure to protect the bodies and clothing from disrespectful visitors who might touch or turn them, with a door that could be locked and guarded.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r5.claim: ‘Their Lord knows them best’ may conclude the builders’ speech, ending the argument, or be a divine parenthesis affirming that God knows what the disputants do not.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r6.claim: Those who prevailed over the affair were the city’s authorities; their decision to make a mosque honored the sleepers and ensured people would keep visiting the cave.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p289/r7.claim: Making mosques over righteous graves was a Christian custom that the Prophet prohibited; ʿĀʾisha said his grave would have been exposed but for that prohibition.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r2.speaker: الراغب
TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r2.claim: Al-Rāghib says ʿathara literally means to stumble and figuratively to learn of something without seeking it; thus God caused people to discover the youths.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r3.claim: As with their awakening, God caused people to discover them; the implied object is the people, and the promise made clear to them is resurrection.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r4.claim: “The Hour has no doubt” explains the promise of God; the people are disputing resurrection, and the dispute's wording signals their concern for it.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r5.claim: The discovery either occurs while people debate resurrection so they learn the promise is true, or is timed to that debate so they learn it then.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r6.claim: Their sleep and awakening parallel death and resurrection: sensation and bodily functions ceased for centuries, yet bodies and clothing remained intact before they returned to their former state.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#15/r7.claim: Both the cave episode and bodily resurrection are extraordinary events; denying them rests on bare incredulity rather than evidence.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r1.claim: The episode occurred amid dispute over resurrection: monotheists affirmed bodily return, while polytheists denied resurrection; the youths’ awakening and death within hours made their case a divine sign by analogy and realization.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r2.claim: One reading takes the first two pronouns in the dispute clause as the townspeople and the third as the youths, with the temporal clause modifying so they would know; the following phrase supports it.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r3.claim: On that reading, the objection that the dispute preceded discovery confuses the earlier resurrection debate with the later dispute about the youths, which occurred after discovery alongside recognition of the sign.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r4.claim: The builders are the polytheists; building a structure over the youths means enclosing them behind a barrier so the public could not inspect them.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r5.claim: The narrative implies that a messenger returned to a transformed, monotheist city after three centuries, crowds investigated the youths, the sign was established, and God took them within hours.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#16/r6.claim: The phrase God knows best indicates that the assembled people disagreed about the youths and some gave up learning their truth.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#17/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#17/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#17/r1.claim: If the dispute concerns resurrection, polytheists dismiss the sign and propose concealing the youths, while monotheists answer that the sign is clear and propose a mosque.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#17/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#17/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#17/r2.claim: If the dispute concerns the youths, people debate whether they are asleep or dead and whether to bury them; polytheists leave them as they are, while monotheists propose a mosque.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#17/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#17/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#17/r3.claim: The resurrection reading best fits the context: the mosque proposal answers the building proposal only if the two factions’ positions conflict, and calling God their Lord suits the polytheists’ speech.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#18/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#18/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#18/r1.claim: Calling the place a mosque identifies those who prevailed as monotheists, since Quranic usage makes a mosque a place for God's remembrance and prostration; the verse is framed as an answer to an implied question.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#18/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#18/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#18/r2.claim: If the affair is the earlier dispute among people, prevailing means the monotheists succeeded through the sign; if it concerns the youths, it may mean those managing their case, with rulers or relatives proposed, the latter being weakest.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#18/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#18/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#18/r3.claim: Other proposed senses make prevailing control of public affairs or authority over what the youths wanted; the possible victors are monotheists, rulers, or officials.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#18/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#18/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#18/r4.claim: Among the proposed explanations of prevailing over their affair, the author judges the first, the monotheists’ victory through the sign, best.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#27/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#27/r5.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:18:9-26#27/r5.claim: The city’s people debated their number but were kept away by fear; the king learned they were believers and proposed a mosque, while the youths asked God to return them to sleep.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#28/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#28/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#28/r5.claim: Some reports say the ruler searched unsuccessfully, others found them asleep and walled up the cave until a shepherd broke in; still others say they met the king and died, or died before his arrival and were hidden, after which a mosque was built.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#30/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#30/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TABATABAI:18:9-26#30/r3.claim: The coin seller alerted officials, who identified the youths from the tablet; the messenger entered the cave while the crowd could not find or enter it, and they built a mosque to pray and seek forgiveness for them.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#31/r4.claim: The report that the cave entrance disappeared from view does not fit its earlier description as visible and known; it raises the question whether God hid and then revealed it.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.claim: The cave story circulated in detailed reports from al-Qummī, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, Ibn Isḥāq, Wahb ibn Munabbih, and al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, among others.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.claim: The transmitted accounts disagree even on major features, while reports about dates, rulers, lineage, appearance, names, and the title أصحاب الرقيم diverge still more.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.claim: One cause is the story’s prominence among People of the Book: Quraysh learned it from them, and its Christian images and monuments spread it widely, so communities reshaped it to fit their beliefs.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.claim: A second cause is Muslims’ broad collection of outside reports, especially through converts such as Wahb ibn Munabbih and Kaʿb al-Aḥbār; later transmitters treated such material as prophetic reports.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.claim: The Qurʾān selects key lessons that serve guidance instead of supplying a complete historical account; it is a book of guidance, not history.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r5.claim: The Qurʾānic narrative first shows the youths’ truth-bearing withdrawal and long sleep, then their awakening and exchange that exposes them, and finally their discovery and the mosque built over them.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.claim: The Qurʾān omits names, ancestry, birth, upbringing, occupations, social standing, dates, rulers, cities, persecutors, and the dog’s identity because guidance does not depend on them; historians and early exegetes filled these gaps, producing divergent accounts.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r3.claim: God allowed their discovery after the persecuting generation and its rule had passed; the new population, dominated by monotheists and disputing resurrection, would receive a sign of it.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r4.claim: The messenger expected the same city, but its people and conditions had changed over three centuries; his old silver exposed him as one of the vanished youths, and the news brought the townspeople to the cave.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r5.claim: The townspeople saw the sign confirming the messenger’s account; the youths soon died, after which polytheists proposed a structure while the monotheists who prevailed proposed a mosque.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.speaker: أهل الرواية والتاريخ
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.claim: Most historians date the story between Jesus and Muḥammad; it is absent from the two Testaments, though some Muslim reports say Quraysh heard it from Jews, while Christians preserved it extensively.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.claim: Christian accounts resemble Ibn Isḥāq’s report from Ibn ʿAbbās in some respects but differ from Muslims on the number of sleepers, whether they had a dog, and the length of their sleep.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#37/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#37/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#37/r5.claim: Ephesus has no mosque or comparable structure by the cave, and no inscription or other evidence identifies its many graves as the sleepers’ or proves their long sleep and awakening.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r3.claim: A Byzantine shrine above the cave was later converted into an Islamic mosque, and another early Muslim mosque stands in the forecourt over a Byzantine church; archaeology dates the shrine to Justin I’s era.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.claim: After centuries as a ruined, forgotten site, Jordanian excavation uncovered Rujayb; the author considers its archaeological signs and some Muslim reports the strongest fit for the Qurʾānic cave.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.claim: Amman stands on the site of Philadelphia, a major and beautiful city before Islam that remained under Roman control from the early second century until the Muslim conquest.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.claim: Other proposed locations include a cave on Mount Qāsiyūn near Damascus, one at Petra, a Scandinavian cave with seven uncorrupted Roman-looking bodies, and a cave near Nakhchivan.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.claim: No evidence identifies any proposed cave as the Qurʾānic one; the Scandinavian and Caucasus claims conflict with the story’s Roman setting and the limits of Roman power.

ASAD-NOTES:18:21#n27/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:21#n27/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:18:21#n27/r1.claim: God draws attention to the story through the legend surrounding the sleepers and the Qur'an's allegorical use of it.

ASAD-NOTES:18:21#n28/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:21#n28/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:18:21#n28/r1.claim: The phrase means that knowledge about the sleepers was made available to others.

ASAD-NOTES:18:21#n29/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:21#n29/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:18:21#n29/r1.claim: The wording indicates that the sleepers' story occupied people for a long time and provoked competing discussions; the next sentence explains its Qur'anic use.

ASAD-NOTES:18:21#n30/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:21#n30/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:18:21#n30/r1.claim: Asad takes alayhim, literally over them, to mean the building is erected over the sleepers in both references.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The verse leaves the exact discovery route unspecified; after investigation, people gradually learned the cave-dwellers' origins, possibly through the market trip.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Islahi infers that once the youths realized their news had spread, they remained in the cave and God caused them to die before people learned their full story.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The cave-dwellers' extraordinary survival offered fresh evidence against disbelievers' doubt about resurrection; God revealed how they lived, making them a public miracle and a story passed on perpetually.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The dispute reflects a reversal: people who persecuted the truthful during life later competed to claim them and worshipped them as idols after death.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: One group favored a memorial while the majority prevailed with a mosque; this suggests the country's majority had become monotheist and the minority was tolerant enough to memorialize them.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The verse suppresses governing nouns in its statements about their Lord knowing them and building a mosque over the cave; calling it a mosque signals monotheism, while later polytheism was a deviation.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:21/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:21/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:21/r1.claim: The youths either died together then or died later as their terms ended, and were buried in the same cave.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:21/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:21/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:21/r2.claim: People debated how long the youths had stayed and what happened to them; some proposed a building above the cave to protect their remains from disturbance, while local rulers proposed a place of worship.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:21/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:21/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:21/r3.claim: Building shrines over good people’s graves became customary and eventually led people to idolatry.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:21/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:21/r4.speaker: Hz. Peygamber
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:21/r4.claim: The Prophet forbade making graves into mosques and censured Jews and Christians for doing so.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r1.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r1.claim: The youths awoke after a shepherd opened the cave while seeking shelter for his flock from rain.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r10.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r10.claim: He presented the youths as proof of bodily and spiritual resurrection, then led people to the cave with the youth.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r11.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r11.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r11.claim: When the youth rejoined the others, they returned to deep sleep; the king and townspeople later found their bodies perfectly preserved.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r12.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r12.speaker: some commentators
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r12.claim: Some versions say the youth spoke briefly with the king and townspeople, bade them well, returned to sleep, and eventually died.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r13.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r13.speaker: some reports
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r13.claim: Some reports say the townsfolk later found tablets listing the youths’ names and story.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r14.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r14.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r14.claim: Their discovery was a sign that God’s promise and the Resurrection are true: raising sleepers unchanged after centuries shows He can raise the dead.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r15.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r15.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r15.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says they built a structure that later became a place for prayer.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r16.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r16.speaker: JJ, R
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r16.claim: Some say believers favored a place of prayer while disbelievers argued for a building as a memorial.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r17.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r17.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r17.claim: Other disputes concerned whether the youths were dead or asleep, their time in the cave, or their number; the people deferred to God’s knowledge.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r7.claim: The old coin exposed the youth; centuries had passed and the city was ruled by the righteous king Tīdhusīs, or Theodocius.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r8.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r8.claim: The townspeople’s dispute concerned whether resurrection restores the body as well as the spirit or raises only the spirit.

STUDYQURAN:18:19/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:19/r9.claim: The righteous king believed in bodily resurrection and prayed for a sign to persuade his people.
